doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Writing lyrics to Milestones for Miles Tones
summary: His creative process: living with a melody for three months, then writing lyrics in half an hour.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: All right. I’m going to try another — whoops wrong button. I’m sure you’ll recognize yourself.
I love it. Tell me about your creative process. This, for those who are watching, this is “Miles Tones.” This is your most recent one, right?

Um hum. Well I have to like the melody. I have to like the melody. Because those are my lyrics to “Milestones.” And I have to like the melody. Because it’s got to be lyrical. It’s got to be singable. It’s got to be hummable. So if I like the melody enough, and I listen to it enough, and then I go by the title. I refer to the title. Right? What’s this about. Well it’s about milestones. What are milestones? Yardsticks? Meters? Inches? Measurement. Can you measure life? And you live with it for a while. The melody. You just keep, I keep listening to it, I keep humming it, and after a while you start to hear words (either that or I’m losing my mind) but you just start to hear a theme in there and then, the encapsulation is it takes me a half an hour to write lyrics to a song. But I listened to it for three months. So I listen to it and listen to it, and it starts to speak, and I start to get a gist of what it means for me.
You know that song has a thing that I wonder, the A section is very up, and then the bridge is much more flowing.
Did that direct your choice of words?
I think it had something to do with it, yeah, I think so. Plus Miles was very lyrical you know, left space to breathe. Left space to think or not think, to just feel it.
